bib.title: TYDI QA: A Benchmark for Information-Seeking Question Answering in Typologically Diverse Languages
bib.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), 2020

read.skipped: Reference list (from char ~50600) skimmed only for lineage.

question: How can one build a trustworthy, translation-free information-seeking QA benchmark that covers typologically diverse languages and measures multilingual progress?
hypothesis: Questions written without seeing the answer, collected natively per language, will have low lexical overlap with answers and yield a harder, more reliable benchmark than translated SQuAD-style data.
contributions: First public large-scale multilingual corpus of information-seeking question-answer pairs, collected without models or translation
11 typologically diverse languages, 204K examples, with linguistic analysis of phenomena
Quantitative data-quality analysis, human-performance estimate, open-source mBERT baseline and a public leaderboard with a hidden test set

method.summary: Annotators write questions from the first 100 characters of a Wikipedia article, a Google search restricted to Wikipedia of that language retrieves the top article, and annotators label a passage answer and a minimal answer span (or NULL, YES/NO). Baselines are a first-passage heuristic and multilingual BERT fine-tuned jointly on all languages.
method.task: information-seeking multilingual QA: passage selection and minimal answer span over full Wikipedia articles

datasets.name: TyDi QA (primary tasks)
datasets.size: 204K examples: 166K one-way annotated train, 37K 3-way annotated dev and test, 277K annotations total
datasets.split: Train 166,916 (1-way); dev 18,670 (3-way); test 18,751 (3-way), over 10 non-English languages plus a small English set; Table 4
datasets.source: Wikipedia atomic snapshots per language; questions written by annotators; 11 languages: English, Arabic, Bengali, Finnish, Indonesian, Japanese, Kiswahili, Korean, Russian, Telugu, Thai
datasets.preprocessing: Tables, long lists and info boxes removed from articles; prompts discarded from final data; dev/test answers verified by a separate annotator pool (except Finnish and Kiswahili)

datasets.name: TyDiQA-GoldP
datasets.split: Only passages with 2+ annotations kept; one annotation withheld as human prediction, rest are gold
datasets.source: Derived from TyDi QA: gold passage only, unanswerable questions dropped, Thai and Japanese removed, SQuAD 1.1 metrics
datasets.preprocessing: 8 languages remain: Arabic, Bengali, Finnish, Indonesian, Kiswahili, Korean, Russian, Telugu

datasets.name: SQuAD v1.1 (English)
datasets.split: Train for the zero-shot GoldP experiment

models.name: mBERT (multilingual BERT, most recently released)
models.architecture: BERT multilingual encoder, setup similar to Alberti et al. (2019), all languages trained jointly in a single model

models.name: First passage
models.architecture: untrained heuristic: always predict the first passage of the article

training.seeds: Primary tasks: mBERT averaged over four fine-tuning replicas; GoldP: averaged over 5 fine tunings

other.fine_tuning: mBERT fine-tuned jointly on all languages of TyDi QA train (primary) or GoldP train; zero-shot variant fine-tuned on English SQuAD 1.1 only. No hyperparameters given.

inference.samples: 4 fine-tuning replicas (primary tasks), 5 fine tunings (GoldP), averaged
inference.retrieval: Article paired to each question by a Google search restricted to the language's Wikipedia domain, top-ranked result

metrics.name: Passage answer F1
metrics.definition: Harmonic mean of precision and recall over examples within a language; credit for matching any annotator-selected passage; NULL consensus requires at least 2 of 3 annotators to select an answer for non-NULL; recall denominator counts non-NULL consensus, precision denominator counts non-NULL predictions

metrics.name: Minimal answer span F1
metrics.definition: Example-wise F1 over byte spans against each annotator's minimal answer with partial credit, max over annotators; YES/NO credit 1.0 if any annotator gave it; scores macro-averaged within language then over non-English languages

metrics.name: Lexical overlap
metrics.definition: Average number of tokens in common between the question and a 200-character window around the answer span, excluding the top 100 most frequent tokens

baselines: Lesser human estimate (1 annotation vs other 2, bootstrap resampled)
eval.protocol: English excluded from macro averages and leaderboard; scores not comparable across languages; hidden test set leaderboard

results.claim: On the minimal answer span task, mBERT overall F1 is far below the lesser human estimate.
results.setup: TyDi QA dev, 10 non-English languages macro-averaged, mBERT jointly fine-tuned, mean of 4 replicas; baseline value is lesser human estimate
results.table: Table 5, row OVERALL, column Minimal Answer mBERT 50.5 vs Human 70.1

results.claim: On passage selection, mBERT overall F1 is well below the human estimate and far above first-passage baseline.
results.setup: TyDi QA, macro-average over 10 non-English languages, mBERT mean of 4 replicas; baseline_value is the lesser human estimate; first-passage baseline is 30.2
results.table: Table 5, row OVERALL, column Passage Answer mBERT 63.1, Lesser Human 79.9, First passage 30.2

results.claim: mBERT fine-tuned on English SQuAD 1.1 only scores much lower on TyDiQA-GoldP than fine-tuned on TyDiQA-GoldP; even English is low.
results.setup: TyDiQA-GoldP dev, 8 languages, mBERT zero-shot from 100k SQuAD 1.1 train, mean of 5 fine tunings; baseline_value is fine-tuned on GoldP; human is 90.9
results.table: Table 7, row OVERALL: GoldP 79.0, SQuAD Zero Shot 56.4, Human 90.9

results.claim: TyDiQA-GoldP has far lower question-answer lexical overlap than MLQA and XQuAD.
results.setup: English; 200-character window around answer, top 100 frequent tokens excluded; TyDiQA-GoldP 0.38, MLQA 0.91, XQuAD 1.52
results.table: Table 6, row (English), columns TYDIQA-GOLDP 0.38, MLQA 0.91, XQuAD 1.52

results.claim: Expert-judged annotation accuracy is high for passage and minimal answers; NULL labels are less accurate.
results.setup: Sample of 200 dev question-answer pairs, Finnish and Russian, judged by trained linguists; NULL 85%, passage answer 92%, minimal answer 93%
results.table: Table 3, column NULL 85%, PASSAGE ANSWER 92%, MINIMAL ANSWER 93%

results.claim: A substantial portion of questions cannot be answered by their article.
results.quote:

results.claim: A single human on Natural Questions short answer scores only 57 F1, used to contextualise TyDi QA human scores.
results.setup: NQ short answer task, single human prediction against five annotations
results.quote:
scores only 57 F1 even with the

limits: Scores are not comparable across languages: each has its own questions, Wikipedia content and annotator quality (Section 7.3)
Human performance is a pessimistic 1-vs-2 estimate that may underestimate since multiple answers can be correct; NQ-style 25-way super-annotation raised estimates by around 15 F1
NULL annotation errors are false positives (missed answers), mitigated by 3-way annotation, but train is only 1-way annotated
Only 11 languages; the authors invite compatible datasets for others
Dev/test answers not separately verified for Finnish and Kiswahili
Only mBERT baseline reported with no fine-tuning hyperparameters; benchmark since superseded by stronger models

terms.definition: a character span that is as short as possible while still forming a satisfactory answer to the question
the asker wants to know the answer but does not know it yet
artifacts introduced by translation, such as preserving source-language word order, making text differ from purely native text
